title: Choose Stories That Illuminate a Pattern
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Choose Stories That Illuminate a Pattern.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Stories preserve context, causality, and human stakes. They can make research memorable, but they must not substitute emotion for evidence. Select a story because it illuminates a pattern, contains a relevant decision or conflict, and represents the conditions the team must understand.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Keep the boundary visible. Explain what the story demonstrates, what corroborates it, and what it does not prove. Protect participants by removing unnecessary identifying detail and avoiding narrative edits that distort their experience.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Select a case for explanatory value
turns.text: What changes when we look at select a case for explanatory value?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team avoids composite stories that blur provenance unless they are clearly labelled and ethically constructed. Identifying detail is removed, participants are not reduced to a dramatic quote, and counter-cases remain visible. Different stories are chosen for different decisions while preserving the same analysis.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at select cases with analytic purpose?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a representative case to make the central pattern concrete, a contrast to reveal conditions, and an edge or negative case to expose limits. State why each was selected. Do not choose only the most emotional quote or construct a composite that implies one person experienced events they did not.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Preserve context: goal, situation, prior knowledge, constraint, action, and consequence. Connect the story to broader evidence and identify whether it illustrates prevalence, mechanism, severity, or possibility. A single story can prove that something occurred, not how common it is.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Protect participants through consent, minimisation, de-identification, and careful handling of distinctive details. Consider how leaders may stereotype a person or group from the story. Pair human detail with structural cause so the burden is not framed as individual deficit.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: End with the decision the pattern informs and evidence needed next. Stories illuminate; they should not manipulate stakeholders into certainty.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Construct a story without manufacturing certainty
turns.text: What changes when we look at construct a story without manufacturing certainty?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Numbers and cases answer different questions. The case explains how and why; distribution shows scope; a negative case tests the explanation. A composite may protect identity or combine recurring detail, but it is explicitly labelled, contains no invented causal event, and links back to the analysis.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Participants’ distinctive words are not reused merely for drama when they increase re-identification or distort meaning.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: failed account recovery?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A dramatic story about one locked-out customer can imply universal system failure. Pairing it with recovery-path data, common mechanisms, and a case that succeeded after human escalation supports a precise decision about where automated recovery ends and accountable support begins.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The most vivid story is rarely automatically the best one. Choose the story that changes a decision while retaining ethical fidelity.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a story to supply the context that a metric, theme, or journey label cannot carry: trigger, goal, constraint, decision, consequence, and recovery. Pair it with the wider evidence pattern and say whether it is typical, illustrative, exceptional, or a counterexample. Edit for clarity without changing the meaning, sequence, or power relationship of the original experience.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The person’s dignity matters more than a more dramatic narrative arc.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Anecdote as prevalence: a vivid incident is treated as evidence of population scale. Context stripping: a quote loses the conditions that explain it. Trauma display: a difficult experience is used for emotional impact without participant care. Story without decision: a narrative is memorable but does not clarify what should change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A team plays a dramatic interview clip about a missed flight. It is powerful, but the situation was unusual. The story earns its place only when it clarifies a broader evidence-backed pattern: people cannot recover when time-sensitive changes are hidden.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 124 calibrated confidence. This lesson makes evidence communicable without inflating certainty. lesson 126 adapts the evidence to the people who must act on it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Take one insight and choose a short incident that illustrates it. Write the evidence pattern below the story and one limit on the claim.
